newsitem.title: UK: Former minister King may enter Conservative race.
newsitem.headline: Former minister King may enter Conservative race.

text.p: A new name on Monday joined the race for the leadership of Britain's defeated Conservative party as the leading candidate faced more controversy.

Tom King, 63, a former defence and Northern Ireland secretary, told a local newspaper he would consider standing for the leadership as a caretaker candidate if the party decided to delay the race to succeed John Major.
But most eyes at Westminster, the home of the Birtish parliament, were focused on a clash expected later in the day between former Home Secretary Michael Howard and his former deputy Ann Widdecombe.
Widdecombe has accused Howard of being "dangerous" and unfit to lead the party.
Widdecombe intends to fuel the row by charging Howard in a debate later on Monday with misleading parliament over the 1995 sacking of prisons boss Derek Lewis after a series of breakouts.

Howard has said he is looking forwrd to answering the charges. But the bitter squabble has overshadowed the contest for the leadership of a party that was dramatically beaten by Labour in the May 1 election.
Faced with a party at war with itself, King told the Western Daily Press of his leadership bid: "It is obviously a tough assignment for anybody.

"If enough people asked me to do it, I would think about it seriously." King -- a Conservative minister without a break from 1979 to 1992 -- said he backed the idea of a caretaker period to allow the party to involve all members in selecting the leader.
Currently, the leader is elected by Conservative MPs. Local associations and members have no vote.
But Labour's landslide victory left the Conservatives -- once renowned as the most successful election-winning machine in the world -- with only 164 surviving MPs.

Other leadership candidates have seized on this, saying lessons should be learned from Prime Minister Tony Blair -- who ruthlessly overhauled Labour, ditching its old socialist credos and introducing more party democracy on its road to power.

Former Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell on Sunday promised an immediate review of the party's structure if he is elected leader and pledged he would put himself up for reelection under the new rules once they were in place next year.
But Dorrell lags Howard and former Welsh Secretary William Hague in the leadership stakes. Widdecombe is supporting former social security secretary Peter Lilley.

Former chancellor of the exchequer Kenneth Clarke is also in the race. He is bitterly opposed by anti-Europeans in the party but he is a doughty political operator and one of the party's best parliamentary performers.
Opinion polls also show Clarke to be the most popular candidate among voters. Whoever wins will have to rebuild the party from its roots and echo the Labour party's drive for younger members.
One Conservative MP, outspoken Euro-sceptic Teresa Gorman, said at the weekend none of the candidates were up to the job.
Gorman, dismissing Hague as a "pre-pubescent political marshmallow", wrote in the Sunday Express: "All the candidates on offer carry too many scars and too much baggage."
